name: Temporal Aliasing Detection
description: Detects temporal aliasing artifacts from frame rate manipulation in AI-generated video sequences.
mechanism:
This method detects AI-generated or manipulated video by analyzing temporal aliasing artifacts — aliasing in the time domain that reveals frame rate manipulation, frame interpolation, or synthetic generation:

1. **Temporal Nyquist Analysis**: Real video cameras sample the visual scene at a fixed frame rate (e.g., 30 fps), creating a temporal sampling that is subject to the Nyquist theorem: any motion faster than half the frame rate (>15 Hz at 30 fps) will be aliased. The method analyzes the temporal frequency content of pixel intensity time series using the temporal DFT. For each pixel, the power spectrum is computed and the energy distribution across temporal frequencies is analyzed. Key diagnostic features include: (a) the temporal Nyquist frequency should match the nominal frame rate (energy should drop sharply at f_s/2), (b) aliased motion (e.g., wagon wheel effect) should be present for fast-moving objects — its absence indicates either very high effective frame rate or synthetic generation, (c) the temporal spectrum should show a natural 1/f falloff (pink noise characteristic) rather than flat or peaked spectra.

2. **Frame Rate Authenticity Verification**: The method verifies that the video's actual temporal sampling matches its declared frame rate. Techniques include: (a) duplicate frame detection — AI generators sometimes produce duplicate frames when upsampling temporal resolution, detected by computing the minimum SSIM between consecutive frames (authentic video rarely produces SSIM > 0.99 except for static scenes), (b) frame interpolation detection — interpolated frames show characteristic 'ghosting' where the intermediate frame blends features from the source frames, producing edge softening that can be detected by comparing edge energy between odd and even frames (periodic pattern indicates interpolation), (c) variable frame rate detection — timestamps embedded in container metadata are compared to actual inter-frame visual differences to detect frame dropping or insertion.

3. **Motion Blur-Frame Rate Coupling**: In real cameras, motion blur is physically coupled to frame rate — the blur extent equals object_velocity × exposure_time, where exposure_time ≤ 1/frame_rate. At 30 fps with 180° shutter angle, the blur for a 10-pixel/frame motion should extend approximately 5 pixels. The method estimates motion velocity from optical flow and measures actual blur from the PSF (point spread function) along the motion direction. Inconsistency between motion blur and frame rate indicates: (a) frame rate conversion (original captured at different fps), (b) AI generation without proper motion blur simulation, (c) post-processing stabilization that altered the exposure model. The blur-velocity ratio should fall within the range [0.3, 0.7] × 1/fps for natural footage.

4. **Temporal Phase Coherence**: The method analyzes the phase structure of the temporal frequency decomposition. In authentic video, the temporal phase evolves linearly with frequency for constant-velocity motion (corresponding to a clean temporal shift). The method computes the temporal phase gradient and checks: (a) phase linearity — R² > 0.9 for constant-velocity segments, (b) phase coherence across spatial neighbors — adjacent pixels with similar motion should show coherent temporal phase, (c) phase discontinuities — abrupt phase jumps indicate frame insertion, deletion, or splicing. AI-generated video often produces temporally incoherent phase because each frame is generated semi-independently, creating phase noise that is absent in naturally-sampled video.
parameters:
Temporal DFT window: 64 frames
Nyquist frequency: f_s/2 (half frame rate)
Duplicate frame threshold: SSIM > 0.99
Edge energy ratio (odd/even): periodic check
Motion blur-velocity ratio: [0.3, 0.7] × 1/fps
Phase linearity threshold: R² > 0.9
Phase coherence: spatial neighbor correlation
1/f spectrum slope: α ≈ 1.0–1.5 (natural video)
Minimum analysis length: 64 frames
Optical flow: Lucas-Kanade for motion estimation
accuracy: 80–89% accuracy detecting AI-generated or frame-manipulated video. Duplicate frame detection achieves AUC of 0.91. Motion blur-frame rate coupling provides F1-score of 0.85. Temporal phase coherence adds 3–5% improvement. Performance highest for videos with visible motion and original frame rates.
source: Wang, W. & Farid, H. (2007). Exposing Digital Forgeries in Video by Detecting Duplication. ACM MM Workshop, 35–42.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated video through temporal sampling artifact analysis. Forensic frame rate manipulation detection. Identifying frame interpolation in deepfake video. Validating temporal authenticity of surveillance footage.
strengths:
• Temporal aliasing is a fundamental physical constraint of real cameras
• Motion blur coupling provides physics-based frame rate verification
• Phase coherence captures generative artifacts invisible in magnitude domain
• Duplicate frame detection is highly reliable for temporal upsampling
• Works independently of video content or scene type
limitations:
• Static scenes produce minimal temporal frequency content
• Global shutter cameras with adjustable exposure complicate blur analysis
• Variable frame rate cameras (some smartphones) add complexity
• Post-processing stabilization can alter temporal characteristics
• High-quality frame interpolation (RIFE, FILM) produces fewer detectable artifacts
